text:
Recently installed emission controls have resulted in a sharp decrease in particulate emissions from aircraft but current emission factors reflect an increase in emissions of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides. With a rapid increase in the number of aircraft using the airfield and with a probable increase in idling times as the field becomes more heavily used, these emissions, added to the emissions of vehicular traffic flowing to and from the airport, may pose a problem, especially in any congested parking area near the terminal. In view of the large tonnage of nitrogen oxides generated by the aircraft, it would seem advisable to include a calculation of vehicular nitrogen oxide emissions in the EIS.
The calculations on pages 92-92C of the statement do not make it clear how much traffic will be noving in the airport area in addition to that using the airport spur and no comment is made on how this traffic can be expected to change in volume between the opening of the spur and 1990.
Local traffic should be taken into account because the air quality near a particular roadway will depend on the total traffic using it.
Another consideration not taken into account in these calculations is the fact that traffic dispersion aids in the dispersion of air pollutants. The five possible corridors and the "no build" alternative are compared on the basis of total tons of carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons emitted per day by the estimated traffic desiring access to the airport from the present interstate system. However it is assumed for corridors 1 and 4 that a portion of this traffic will take a route to the terminal other than the proposed spur, and with the no build alternative the traffic is dispersed over four different, partially overlapping routes. Hence in terms of local pollutant concentrations, these alternatives are not strictly comparable to the other three corridors and, in particular, the favored corridor 5 is not strictly comparable to the no build alternative.
A "worst case" calculation should be carried out for the air quality along the airport spur. Since the most stringent emission controls are not required on new automobiles until 1976, the vorst case might occur soon after the spur opens, during peak traffic flow. If it is still possible that the spur will be open by late 1975, a calculation should be done for this year. The traffic data needed would include the projected peak hourly flow, the time at which it occurs, the associated average traffic speed and the heavy-duty vehicle mix broken down into gasoline powered and diesel powered vehicles. The expected eight-hour traffic maximum would also be useful. In addition, a calculation should be made for off-peak traffic conditions. A liaison meeting between several staff members from the Department of Transportation and the Department of Natural Resources Air Pollution Control Section was held on September 6 to discuss such calculations.
